title: OpenAI rewrites its usage policy to ban distillation into rival models and vet third-party routers
subtitle: The updated policy, effective November 20, forbids using OpenAI outputs to train competing models and requires prior approval for gateways and resellers that expose OpenAI models to third parties.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI's revised usage policies, which went into effect on November 20, add explicit anti-distillation language and a new approval regime for intermediaries. The core clause says users may not use OpenAI models or their outputs to generate, prepare, select, or supply training material or signals for models that are intended as alternatives to or substitutes for OpenAI models or services. OpenAI frames the restriction as a safety measure: training a rival on OpenAI outputs can transfer capability without carrying the safeguards across. A separate clause now requires services that give third parties direct access to OpenAI models — routers, gateways and resellers — to get OpenAI's prior review and approval, though the rule does not apply to applications that simply integrate OpenAI to power their own features.

The policy keeps carveouts. Research, software development and model evaluation are still permitted within the new boundaries, and OpenAI says it will approve specific partners case by case to use its models for otherwise prohibited tasks. National security and law enforcement uses get a similar case-by-case review of proposed use and safeguards. The change mirrors a tightening at Anthropic in October and comes after CISA warned that Chinese developers — DeepSeek, Moonshot, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.ai among them — had allegedly distilled both OpenAI and Anthropic models.

Distillation has moved from a research-paper topic to a trade-policy fault line this year. Anthropic said in October that its own distillation defenses cut harvested data by 90 to 99 percent and that it had banned tens of thousands of accounts tied to campaigns from Chinese labs. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned in July of possible sanctions tied to the practice. OpenAI's new policy pulls the same lever on the contract side: even if a scraper evades the technical defenses, the terms of service now give OpenAI a basis to sue, revoke keys and refer cases to US authorities.

A note for learners: the barrier that matters for a frontier lab is no longer a benchmark score — it's the chain of licenses, contracts and defenses that keep its model weights and outputs out of a competitor's training set. If you are learning how modern AI businesses work, read the usage policy of the model you use. It will tell you more about where the industry thinks its moat lives than any datasheet.
